KRA Explains Reverse Invoicing for Kenyan Farmers to Meet eTIMS Requirements
items.description: Kenya Revenue Authority’s reverse invoicing lets factories issue eTIMS invoices for farmers, with consent, SMS alerts and buyer-paid costs easing compliance.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) unveiled a reverse invoicing arrangement under which factories and other agricultural produce buyers can generate electronic tax invoices on behalf of small-scale farmers, removing the need for individual farmers to operate their own invoicing systems.
KRA Commissioner for Micro and Small Taxpayers George Obell announced the arrangement at the KRA Citizen Assembly, a taxpayer town hall held at Murang'a University on Tuesday, November 17, 2026.

Obell said the arrangement addresses a persistent challenge in agricultural supply chains where large processors deal with numerous smallholder suppliers who may lack the equipment, internet connectivity, or technical know-how to issue eTIMS invoices independently.
KRA issues November 20 deadline for 5 key taxes: Here’s what you need to know
Under the arrangement, an approved buyer such as a dairy processor documents the transaction directly within eTIMS, capturing details including the quantity of produce received and the agreed price.

A dairy factory buying milk from smallholder farmers, for instance, can generate an invoice reflecting each delivery without requiring each farmer to maintain a separate invoicing system.
This benefits buyers as well, since the generated invoices serve as valid documentation to support expense claims when filing tax returns.
Before any buyer can use the system, KRA requires them to complete a Know Your Customer process and obtain explicit approval from the authority.
Farmers must give informed consent before invoices can be raised in their name, and they receive notifications by SMS or email each time a transaction is recorded.
Inua Jamii registration 2026: Who qualifies, requirements and how to apply
Farmers can also independently monitor and validate invoices through their eTIMS dashboard.
Buyers are required to capture the farmer's KRA PIN, the quantity supplied, and the transaction price, and must maintain a full audit trail of all records.
KRA also stipulates that buyers must absorb the operational costs of the reverse invoicing functionality rather than passing them on to farmers.
The arrangement is not entirely new. KRA introduced reverse invoicing on December 27, 2024, initially capturing transactions worth KSh 800 million.
At that point, approximately 800 buyers had used the system to generate around 4,500 invoices for small suppliers.

The renewed push comes after KRA issued a public notice on November 10, 2025, confirming that from January 1, 2026, declared income and expenses in tax returns would be validated against eTIMS records.
That requirement exposed a documentation gap for businesses buying produce from farmers unable to issue compliant electronic invoices.

Reverse invoicing is positioned as one of several solutions, alongside eTIMS Lite services accessible through eCitizen and USSD, designed to draw informal and small-scale suppliers into the electronic tax framework.
Obell encouraged farmers encountering difficulties with the process to contact KRA offices or reach out through the authority's official communication channels for assistance.

items.title: Zimbabwean Billionaire Seeks KSh 129b to Fund Chips in Kenya, Other African Markets
items.description: Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa's Cassava Technologies is courting US and Middle East investors for up to $1bn (KSh129bn) to buy Nvidia chips.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

Elijah Ntongai is an experienced editor at TUKO.co.ke, with more than four years in financial, business, labour and technology research and reporting. His work provides valuable insights into Kenyan, African, and global trends.

Cassava Technologies, the pan-African digital infrastructure company founded by Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa, is in private discussions with potential investors in the United States and the Middle East to raise up to KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion).

As reported first by Bloomberg, the capital is intended to fund the purchase of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), the semiconductors that power modern AI systems, and to strengthen the company's fibre-optic and data centre networks to meet rising demand for AI computing across Africa.

Should the raise succeed, it would add to an already substantial investment drive at Cassava. The company has committed to deploying 12,000 Nvidia chips across planned AI facilities in South Africa , Egypt, Kenya, and Nigeria as part of a wider KSh 93 billion (USD 720 million) programme to establish five AI computing hubs on the continent.

A facility in Cape Town is already operational, with additional locations planned in Johannesburg, Egypt, Kenya, Morocco, and Nigeria .

Separately, Cassava is partnering with Vodafone Business and Egyptian industrial group Elsewedy Electric on a KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion) data centre development in Egypt, which will include the country's first sovereign AI data centre.
The project is expected to begin with 20 megawatts of capacity and scale to 200 megawatts over time, potentially creating around 200 direct jobs and 2,000 indirect ones.

Cassava holds the distinction of being Nvidia's first cloud partner based in Africa. Both Google and Nvidia are among its existing shareholders, connecting the company to two of the most influential players in global AI.
Elon Musk's Starlink banned from operating in top African country
Masiyiwa, born in 1961, built his business empire through Econet Wireless after a prolonged legal fight to obtain a mobile operating licence in Zimbabwe.

Cassava Technologies was later established as a separate pan-African platform encompassing Liquid Intelligent Technologies, which operates more than 116,000 kilometres of fibre-optic network, and Africa Data Centres. Forbes estimates his net worth at $2.2 billion as of 2026.

The KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion) figure represents a fundraising target, not money already secured, and the discussions may not result in a completed deal. If finalised, it would rank among the largest private capital raises for digital infrastructure in African history.
The fundraising effort comes as Nvidia navigates a period of internal turbulence.
Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president and chief executive on November 12, 2026, following revelations of a personal scandal.

CFO Colette Kress has assumed the role of interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement. More than 158,000 people, including over 7,500 self-identified Nvidia employees, signed an open letter calling for Huang's reinstatement by November 15, with Elon Musk among those publicly backing the campaign.

Nvidia has stated that its operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap will continue uninterrupted.
No African partner, including Cassava, has announced any project delays linked to the leadership transition.

content: From fashion and handmade crafts to interior design and lifestyle content, Kenyan entrepreneurs are increasingly using social media to turn creative ideas into businesses, tapping into audiences that extend beyond traditional marketplaces.

Platforms such as TikTok have changed how consumers discover products, interact with brands and make purchasing decisions. For many small businesses, a compelling video or a well-told brand story can now be as important as having a physical shop.

This shift was among the issues explored at a Nairobi gathering on Wednesday, November 18, organised by TikTok and the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) as they launched the Digital Commerce Labs, an initiative intended to equip small businesses across Sub-Saharan Africa with digital commerce skills.
TikTok’s Head of Global Institution Engagement, Kushal Prakash, said the initiative was intended to help entrepreneurs benefit from the changing digital marketplace.

“We have seen how TikTok makes it easier for businesses to be discovered and influence purchase decisions through trends such as #TikTokMadeMeBuyIt. Social commerce has the power to unlock opportunities, level the playing field and equip Kenyan entrepreneurs with the tools to grow.”

In attendance to share their stories were content creators Cherie Kihato, founder of Savannah Space and a TikTok 2026 Global Discover List creator; Alix, founder of Mammacita in Pink; and Emmy Rono, Executive Director of Urembo Craft who shared their experiences of using digital content to communicate their brands, showcase their offerings and connect with potential customers.

Using their experiences, the forum aimed to showcase the wider change in how businesses approach marketing. Beyond advertising products, entrepreneurs are increasingly required to create content that tells stories, builds communities and gives audiences a reason to engage with their brands.

Dr Caroline Kaua, Director of Business Development, Marketing and Trade at the Micro and Small Enterprises Authority, said businesses needed the skills to adapt as digital platforms changed how consumers discovered and purchased products.

“Micro, small and medium enterprises play an important role in Kenya’s economy, creating jobs, supporting livelihoods and driving entrepreneurship,” she said. “As digital transformation continues to change how consumers discover and purchase products, it is important that our MSMEs have the skills and tools to adapt and take advantage of these changes.” According to a GSMA survey, 49 per cent of Kenyan businesses sell online exclusively through social media, while another 13 per cent combine social platforms with a website or online marketplace.
More than 40 per cent of internet users in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa have also purchased products through social commerce platforms.

However, converting online attention into sustainable business growth requires more than simply posting regularly. Entrepreneurs need to understand their audiences, develop engaging content and identify ways to turn digital interactions into sales.

The programme will offer online learning modules and virtual, trainer-led sessions covering digital presence, content creation, artificial intelligence-driven e-commerce tools and strategies for reaching domestic and international markets.
ICC Deputy Secretary General Julian Kassum said digital commerce could create new opportunities for entrepreneurship, trade and job creation.

“Digital commerce is a powerful engine for inclusive growth. By equipping small businesses with the tools and skills they need to participate in the digital economy, we are opening new pathways for entrepreneurship, trade and job creation.”

items.title: Not safe: New study raises alarm over findings on chicken meat sold in Nairobi
items.description: A Kenya Veterinary Association study finds harmful bacteria in Nairobi chicken outlets, revealing widespread hygiene failures and antimicrobial resistance risks.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

Almost all raw chicken meat sold at butcheries and non-supermarket retail outlets across Nairobi County is contaminated with harmful bacteria, according to a new study by the Kenya Veterinary Association (KVA).

The study, conducted by the KVA Technical Working Group on Processing, Food Security and Safety, and Quality Assurance in collaboration with the Department of Public Health, Pharmacology and Toxicology at the University of Nairobi , assessed 264 retail establishments.
Researchers collected chicken meat samples and tested them for three pathogens while also interviewing vendors about their storage, handling, and hygiene practices.
NTSA issues festive season safety alert, lists what officers will check on roads

Escherichia coli was detected in 94.7% of samples. Staphylococcus aureus was present in 39.3% of samples, and Salmonella in 8.1%. Co-contamination with both E. coli and S. aureus was recorded in 34% of cases.
PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
The hygiene data collected from the outlets helps explain the scale of the problem.
Some 92.8% of establishments used wooden chopping boards, which are porous and resistant to thorough cleaning.
Seven in ten outlets had no handwashing facility, and 54.6% stored chicken at room temperature rather than under refrigeration.
Surfaces with visible meat and blood residue were observed in 75% of establishments, while only 9.9% of attendants were seen wearing clean protective clothing.

Most chicken arrived at retail points fresh and warm, with 92.4% of outlets receiving unchilled meat. Around 79.2% of outlets sourced stock from distributors or wholesalers, and 47% sourced from local farms.

The study also identified significant antimicrobial resistance among the bacteria isolated. Some 44.7% of E. coli isolates and 28.4% of S. aureus isolates were classified as multidrug-resistant, meaning they resisted three or more classes of antibiotics.
Kenyans advise Saudi returnee earning KSh 70k on best business ideas, suggest several
E. coli showed high resistance to cotrimoxazole at 65.9% and ampicillin at 50.8%. Salmonella isolates displayed low resistance levels overall, with 99.6% classified as non-multidrug-resistant.

Statistical analysis identified specific practices linked to higher contamination risk. Chicken handled on shared surfaces carried more than three times the odds of E. coli contamination compared with meat handled on dedicated surfaces.
The use of wooden chopping boards was associated with more than three times higher odds of S. aureus contamination.
Meat sourced through middlemen faced higher odds of Salmonella contamination, while freezer storage was linked to 72% lower odds of Salmonella presence.
Attendants with college or university education were associated with significantly lower odds of contamination across all three pathogens.
KVA National President Kelvin Osore said the findings highlight an urgent need to strengthen food safety standards across the entire poultry supply chain.
The KVA is recommending that the government introduce mandatory food safety training for meat handlers, enforce cold-chain standards, and conduct routine microbial surveillance.
Nairobi County expands newborn intensive care units to boost premature baby survival
Retailers are urged to replace wooden boards with stainless steel or food-grade plastic surfaces and ensure functioning handwashing stations with soap and clean water.
County governments are advised to develop localised food safety policies and strengthen inspection services, while consumers are encouraged to demand safe food and practise proper handling at home.

The footage shared on October 28, 2026, shows her walking through rows of multi-tiered cages, gathering fresh eggs and placing them in trays, although she did not disclose the farm's location, number of birds or daily production figures.

Accompanying the video with a gospel track, Omanga described hard work and honest hustling as important values beyond political leadership, saying she believes in serving people through productive activities.
The showcase attracted attention from social media users, with many praising her for highlighting agribusiness as a source of income and an alternative professional pursuit outside politics .

items.title: How to Spot Fake Study-Abroad Agents: 10 Warning Signs You Should Never Ignore
items.description: Learn how students can spot scams, verify recruiters and protect their money from fraud in Kenya. Kenya’s CUE requires study-abroad agents to hold valid licences.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)
Kenyan students and their families are increasingly falling prey to fraudulent study-abroad agents who exploit the growing demand for overseas education.
This has prompted regulators to issue fresh warnings about the scale of the problem.
The Commission for University Education (CUE), empowered under the Universities Act, mandates that all student recruitment agencies operating in Kenya must be duly registered, vetted and licensed.
Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)
CUE publicly maintains a register of approved consultants, searchable by name, branch and licence expiry date.
Any agent whose name does not appear on that list, or whose licence cannot be independently verified, is operating illegally.
Inua Jamii registration 2026: Who qualifies, requirements and how to apply
CUE has also previously warned that degrees obtained from universities not on its approved list will not be recognised in Kenya.
Beyond the licence check, students should be alert to agents who claim guaranteed admission, visas or scholarships.
No legitimate agent anywhere in the world can promise a visa outcome; that decision rests solely with the relevant embassy based on official criteria.
For example, the US and Canada's immigration authorities have stated plainly that any offer of a "special visa deal" or "guaranteed approval" is a fraud.
Requests for large upfront payments sent to personal M-Pesa numbers or private bank accounts are a consistent warning sign.
Genuine fees should be paid directly to the university or the relevant government portal, and official receipts on company letterhead must be provided for every transaction.

Other warning signs include offers of fully-funded scholarships that require an application fee (legitimate scholarships are free to apply for), unfamiliar or unaccredited institutions named in offer letters, and study packages that emphasise full-time work over education.
Public Procurement Regulatory Authority advertises 35 jobs for compliance officers, other positions
Student visas almost universally restrict working hours, so any pitch centred on guaranteed employment abroad should be treated with deep scepticism.

Agents who apply high-pressure tactics, such as claiming only a few spots remain or demanding payment within hours, are using classic manipulation techniques designed to prevent students from doing proper research.
Agent not on CUE's register, or licence cannot be verified
Check the CUE licensed-agency list before paying anything
Guaranteed admission, visa or scholarship
Claims of "100% visa success", "guaranteed admission", "special deals"
Walk away — only universities and embassies decide these
Cash or M-Pesa payments to an individual, not the institution
Pay tuition only to the university's official portal or account
"Fully funded" scholarships requiring a fee; high-paying jobs bundled with study
Verify directly with the university or government website; never pay to "secure" a scholarship
Unfamiliar school, unaccredited institution, unsolicited admission letter
Confirm the offer by emailing the university's admissions office using its official contact details
Promise of full-time work alongside study
Remember student visas restrict work hours; treat it as a job scam
"Only two spots left", "act today", nonstop calls, short deadlines
Slow down — legitimate programmes allow time to verify
WhatsApp/Facebook only, no physical address, hidden company details
Ask for registered office and licence details; visit in person if possible
Fake bank statements, sponsor letters, transcripts, coaching to lie
Refuse — fake documents lead to refusal, bans, and legal trouble
Verbal agreements, vague pricing, no cancellation clause
Insist on a signed contract with clear fees and refund terms; keep all receipts
Kenya Industrial Estates advertises 38 jobs, how to apply
Perhaps the most dangerous sign is an agent who encourages a student to submit false bank statements, forged transcripts or fabricated sponsor letters.
Using fraudulent documents can result in permanent visa bans, regardless of whether the student was aware of the falsification.

If fraud is suspected, students should stop all payments immediately, preserve all evidence, including screenshots and receipts, and file a report with the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI).
CUE should also be notified if the agent claimed to be licensed. Applying directly through a university's official website, without any agent, remains the safest option available.

In other news, the European Union offers Kenyan graduates fully funded master's scholarships under the Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters programme, providing a monthly stipend of €1,400 (approximately KSh 196,000) for up to 24 months.

The scholarship covers tuition and participation fees, health insurance, and contributions towards travel and relocation costs, with students studying at university consortia across multiple European countries.

Applications for the 2027–2029 intake are open through individual programme portals, with deadlines ranging from December 2026 to February 2027, including Neurasmus on December 1, EMMIR on December 20, GLOBE on January 4 and InterMaths on February 17.

Applicants must hold a bachelor's degree or recognised equivalent and submit documents such as academic transcripts, certificates, a CV, motivation letter and academic references, although individual programmes may impose additional requirements.

MSEA backs digital push to help Kenyan MSMEs expand online markets
items.description: The Micro and Small Enterprises Authority (MSEA) has stepped up efforts to boost digital entrepreneurship following the launch of a new programme aimed
content: The Micro and Small Enterprises Authority (MSEA) has stepped up efforts to boost digital entrepreneurship following the launch of a new programme aimed at helping small businesses harness online platforms to grow their enterprises and reach wider markets.

The initiative, dubbed TikTok/International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Digital Commerce Labs (DCL), seeks to equip entrepreneurs, particularly women and young people, with practical digital skills to improve their online visibility, attract customers and increase sales.

The programme was officially launched by MSEA Director of Business Development, Marketing and Trade, Dr Caroline Kaua, alongside the Head of Presidential Special Projects and Creative Economy, Dennis Itumbi.

The launch attracted representatives from the private sector, business associations, digital creators and entrepreneurs, including partners such as TikTok, ICC Kenya, the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI) and the Kenya Private Sector Alliance (KEPSA).

Speaking at the event, Itumbi applauded TikTok and ICC Kenya for introducing the initiative, noting that entrepreneurs also need to understand how to safeguard their innovations, business ideas and intellectual property as they expand into the digital space.

He further urged TikTok to explore the possibility of introducing TikTok Shops in Kenya, saying the platform could create additional opportunities for businesses to sell their products online and reach customers beyond the country’s borders.
EALA proposes regional law to protect traditional seeds
On her part, Dr Kaua reaffirmed MSEA’s commitment to strengthening small businesses through digital transformation, improved market access and initiatives that enhance their competitiveness.

She pointed to opportunities for integrating the programme with existing government interventions, including the National Youth Opportunities Towards Advancement (NYOTA) programme, Kenya Jobs and Economic Transformation (KJET) project and Uwezo Fund.
Kaua also proposed leveraging MSEA’s registration framework through the Registrar of Micro and Small Enterprises to bring more businesses on board and widen the programme’s reach.

She challenged entrepreneurs to move beyond simply establishing an online presence and focus on converting digital engagement into tangible business results. This, she noted, requires creating engaging content, understanding consumer preferences and building customer confidence to turn online interactions into actual purchases.

Implemented in collaboration with ICC Kenya, the Digital Commerce Labs will provide entrepreneurs with a broader learning platform through practical training, strategic partnerships and engagement with digital content creators.

The initiative comes amid growing opportunities for small businesses to use digital platforms to promote their products, connect with consumers and explore markets that would otherwise be difficult to access.
MSEA said it remains committed to supporting enterprises to embrace innovation, strengthen their operations and take advantage of emerging opportunities in the digital economy.

Nairobi Water has issued a public notice advising customers that its billing system will be taken offline for scheduled maintenance from Friday, November 20, 2026, through Monday, November 23, 2026.

The planned downtime, confirmed through an official notice from the company's Corporate Affairs and Liaison Department, will begin at 3:00 PM on November 20 and run until 8:00 AM on November 23, spanning approximately 65 hours.

Throughout the maintenance window, four core service functions will be unavailable: customer contracting, meter reading, billing, and revenue collection.
This means customers will not be able to pay water bills, register new accounts, or request meter readings during that period. Automated invoice generation will also be paused.
Nairobi Water said the shutdown is required to upgrade and improve its systems. "Kindly complete any necessary transactions before the planned maintenance," the notice stated.

Content creator Mungai Eve has gone public with details of her hair restoration journey after a consultation at a clinic revealed more than she had bargained for.

In a video shared on November 17, Eve sat with a doctor who examined her scalp using a head-mounted dermatoscope, walking her through the results of an earlier scan in a candid session that she chose to bring her audience into.

Eve had initially come in dealing with traction alopecia, a form of hair loss caused by physical manipulation of the hair. However, the scan uncovered a separate and more complex condition called CCCA, Central Centrifugal Cicatricial Alopecia, an inflammatory condition of the scalp that the doctor described as very common among African men and women.

His point was clear: the inflammation at the crown of Eve's scalp needs to be fully under control before any transplant procedure can go ahead.

The plan going forward is for her to complete the medical therapy before returning to discuss the hairline transplant as the next step.

Popular Kenyan content creator Baba Talisha has shared a devastating health update with his followers, confirming that he has permanently lost sight in one of his eyes.

The content creator had been fighting a rare parasitic eye infection called Acanthamoeba Keratitis, a notoriously difficult condition to diagnose.
He previously revealed that he endured more than 14 medical tests before doctors could identify what was attacking his eye.

His wife, Miss Wanjey, shed more light on the situation during a TikTok livestream on November 11, explaining that the amoeba had burrowed into the cornea, where it forms cysts and keeps multiplying, making treatment extremely complicated.

She also disclosed that medical teams had been treating the wrong condition for close to two months, giving the infection a dangerous window to advance. That delay is what ultimately caused his left eye to turn visibly white and robbed him of all sight in it.
Baba Talisha has confirmed that surgery is on the horizon, and he is now preparing to travel to India for specialist medical attention.

items.description: Organisation: Amnesty International KenyaOpportunity: Call for SubmissionsConference: East Africa Data Governance Conference 2027Theme: Designed for Whom?
content: Organisation: Amnesty International Kenya Opportunity: Call for Submissions Conference: East Africa Data Governance Conference 2027 Theme: Designed for Whom? Trust, Accountability, and the Citizen at the Centre of Data Governance Sector: Technology, Human Rights, Digital Rights, Data Governance and Public Policy Submission Deadline: 11 December 2026 Deadline Time: 5:00 PM East Africa Time (EAT) Conference Year: 2027 Submission Formats: Presentations, Discussions, Panels, Roundtables and Workshops
Amnesty International Kenya is part of the global Amnesty International movement, working to promote and protect human rights, freedom, dignity and justice.

Through research, advocacy, public engagement and strategic partnerships, the organisation works to address human rights violations and strengthen accountability among governments, institutions and other powerful actors.
Its work on technology and human rights focuses on emerging challenges associated with digital transformation, data protection, online freedoms, privacy and responsible technology governance.
As part of its commitment to advancing digital rights and citizen-centred policies, Amnesty International Kenya is inviting submissions for the East Africa Data Governance Conference 2027.

The East Africa Data Governance Conference 2027 will bring together researchers, practitioners, policymakers, innovators, journalists, civil society organisations and community leaders to explore critical issues surrounding data governance in the region.

Under the theme Designed for Whom? Trust, Accountability, and the Citizen at the Centre of Data Governance , the conference aims to promote discussions and solutions that place citizens’ rights, interests and lived experiences at the centre of data governance systems.

The conference provides a platform for participants to exchange research findings, share practical experiences, present innovative solutions and develop recommendations that strengthen transparency, accountability and responsible data management.
Contributors from different professional backgrounds are encouraged to submit their ideas, research and experiences.
The call for submissions is open to individuals and organisations working in areas related to technology, data governance, human rights, policy development and digital transformation.
Both established professionals and individuals with practical community-level experience are encouraged to contribute.
Amnesty International Kenya is particularly interested in submissions that demonstrate practical relevance, original thinking and opportunities for improving data governance across East Africa.
Proposals should aim to achieve one or more of the following:
Submissions should demonstrate how their ideas can contribute to more inclusive, accountable and citizen-centred data governance systems.
Applicants can select the format that best communicates their research, experience or proposed contribution.
This format is designed for contributors interested in presenting research findings, projects, case studies or practical experiences.
Presentations provide an opportunity to share evidence, discuss findings and demonstrate practical solutions to data governance challenges.
This format allows contributors to facilitate interactive conversations around important data governance issues.
Participants can use this format to explore emerging challenges, exchange perspectives and encourage collaborative problem-solving.
Discussion sessions should promote active engagement and meaningful participation.
The panel format is intended for discussions involving experts with different professional backgrounds and perspectives.
Panels are suitable for examining complex policy questions, technological developments and accountability challenges.
The roundtable format provides a moderated environment for collaborative discussion and participant engagement.
It is suitable for contributors seeking to bring together different stakeholders to exchange experiences, identify shared challenges and explore possible solutions.
The workshop format combines short presentations with practical, interactive group activities.
Workshops are particularly appropriate for practical learning, collaborative exercises, skills development and exploring innovative approaches to data governance.

items.description: Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa's Cassava Technologies is courting US and Middle East investors for up to $1bn (KSh129bn) to buy Nvidia chips.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

Elijah Ntongai is an experienced editor at TUKO.co.ke, with more than four years in financial, business, labour and technology research and reporting. His work provides valuable insights into Kenyan, African, and global trends.

Cassava Technologies, the pan-African digital infrastructure company founded by Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa, is in private discussions with potential investors in the United States and the Middle East to raise up to KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion).

As reported first by Bloomberg, the capital is intended to fund the purchase of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), the semiconductors that power modern AI systems, and to strengthen the company's fibre-optic and data centre networks to meet rising demand for AI computing across Africa.
TikTok, ICC launch commerce labs to train Kenyan small businesses with growth skills

Should the raise succeed, it would add to an already substantial investment drive at Cassava. The company has committed to deploying 12,000 Nvidia chips across planned AI facilities in South Africa , Egypt, Kenya, and Nigeria as part of a wider KSh 93 billion (USD 720 million) programme to establish five AI computing hubs on the continent.

A facility in Cape Town is already operational, with additional locations planned in Johannesburg, Egypt, Kenya, Morocco, and Nigeria .

Separately, Cassava is partnering with Vodafone Business and Egyptian industrial group Elsewedy Electric on a KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion) data centre development in Egypt, which will include the country's first sovereign AI data centre.
The project is expected to begin with 20 megawatts of capacity and scale to 200 megawatts over time, potentially creating around 200 direct jobs and 2,000 indirect ones.

Cassava holds the distinction of being Nvidia's first cloud partner based in Africa. Both Google and Nvidia are among its existing shareholders, connecting the company to two of the most influential players in global AI.
Elon Musk's Starlink banned from operating in top African country
Masiyiwa, born in 1961, built his business empire through Econet Wireless after a prolonged legal fight to obtain a mobile operating licence in Zimbabwe.

Cassava Technologies was later established as a separate pan-African platform encompassing Liquid Intelligent Technologies, which operates more than 116,000 kilometres of fibre-optic network, and Africa Data Centres. Forbes estimates his net worth at $2.2 billion as of 2026.

The KSh 129 billion (USD 1 billion) figure represents a fundraising target, not money already secured, and the discussions may not result in a completed deal. If finalised, it would rank among the largest private capital raises for digital infrastructure in African history.
The fundraising effort comes as Nvidia navigates a period of internal turbulence.
Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president and chief executive on November 12, 2026, following revelations of a personal scandal.

CFO Colette Kress has assumed the role of interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement. More than 158,000 people, including over 7,500 self-identified Nvidia employees, signed an open letter calling for Huang's reinstatement by November 15, with Elon Musk among those publicly backing the campaign.

Nvidia has stated that its operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap will continue uninterrupted.
No African partner, including Cassava, has announced any project delays linked to the leadership transition.

items.title: Kenyans Could Soon Convert Petrol Cars Into Electric Vehicles Without Buying New Ones
items.description: Kenya’s Transport Ministry is exploring EV retrofitting that could let motorists convert petrol and diesel cars to electric without buying new vehicles.
content: The Ministry of Transport is exploring new electric vehicle retrofitting technology that will allow Kenyan motorists to convert their petrol and diesel cars into electric vehicles without buying new ones.

This proposal emerged on Wednesday, November 18, following high-level discussions between Transport Principal Secretary Joseph Mbugua and Euro Retrofits Mobility President Emmanuel Flahaut. During the meeting, Flahaut demonstrated how electric vehicle retrofitting works and outlined strategies for introducing the green mobility solution to the Kenyan market.

The conversion process removes a vehicle’s traditional internal combustion engine and replaces it with an electric motor and battery pack. By upgrading existing cars to run on electricity, Kenyan drivers can bypass the prohibitive cost of spending millions of shillings on brand-new electric vehicles.

Flahaut informed ministry officials that the retrofitting technology adapts easily across multiple transport categories, including motorcycles, private cars, buses, delivery vans, trucks, and other commercial fleets. Depending on the vehicle class and the complexity of the engineering required, technicians can complete a full conversion in anywhere from a single day to three weeks.
Ministry officials noted that adopting EV retrofitting will extend the lifespan of existing vehicles while shielding motorists from volatile petrol and diesel prices.

Principal Secretary Mbugua added that transitioning older vehicles to electric power will significantly curb air pollution, particularly in congested urban centers where thousands of fuel-powered vehicles emit daily exhaust fumes. These talks align with Kenya’s broader national push to accelerate electric mobility adoption and transition away from fossil fuel transport.

content: The 2026/2027 mass mosquito net distribution campaign across 18 malaria-endemic counties has kicked off.

The Ministry of Health says it will distribute 10.8 million insecticide-treated mosquito nets in 99 sub-counties under the Kenya Malaria Strategy, in a move aimed at protecting families, reducing malaria infections and accelerating the country’s progress towards malaria elimination.

A key feature of this year’s campaign is the deployment of the DigiMO, a digital platform to strengthen household verification, beneficiary identification, distribution tracking and real-time monitoring.

To address insecticide resistance, the campaign will also introduce next-generation dual active ingredient insecticide-treated nets (dual-AI ITNs) in areas where mosquitoes have developed resistance to conventional insecticides, enhancing the effectiveness of malaria prevention.

Public Health and Professional Standards Principal Secretary Mary Muthoni says the campaign reinforces the Government’s preventive and promotive healthcare agenda under Universal Health Coverage (UHC), bringing essential health interventions closer to households and communities.

“As the country intensifies its efforts towards malaria elimination, communities are urged to participate in the exercise, collect their allocated nets and sleep under them every night throughout the year,” she said.
She noted that the fight against the killer disease requires collective responsibility, sustained investment and strong partnerships.
“Together, we can protect households, save lives and accelerate Kenya’s journey towards a malaria-free future.”

The campaign comes against the backdrop of gains made under the Kenya Malaria Strategy 2023–2027, with the country recording a 34 per cent decline in confirmed malaria cases, from 5.54 million in 2023 to 3.64 million in the latest reported year.
Despite the progress, malaria remains a significant public health challenge in Kenya, affecting millions of people annually, particularly in regions with sustained transmission.
Malaria incidence among children under five has also declined from 194 to 119 cases per 1,000 population, while testing now reaches nearly 90 per cent of suspected malaria cases.
“These gains reflect sustained investments in prevention, testing, treatment, surveillance and community-based healthcare interventions,” she said.

Muthoni added that the allocation of mosquito nets is guided by population needs, malaria transmission patterns and insecticide resistance profiles to ensure communities receive nets suited to their prevailing malaria risks.
